Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: The High Court is required to authorize material changes in birth/death registrations and name changes. The National Registration Act provides for court recourse for denied registrations and criminal offences related to fraudulent registration. However, there are no ID-specific judicial mechanisms or dedicated ID courts.

revision_notes: Confirmed. Fetched the 2018 ID4D diagnostic (still live) and found a real High Court case (ND v Attorney General, Registrar of National Registration) that reviewed a Registrar decision under the National Registration Act, corroborating that ordinary judicial review applies to ID decisions but no ID-specific court/mechanism exists. Code 2 stands.

Definition: Whether the system and the production of credentials can be managed, maintained and developed by in-country technical staff (as opposed to foreign vendors)
Comments: DCNR (Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs) handles administrative functions including card production, enrollment, and data management. However, system maintenance and technical support is contracted to external (largely foreign) vendors at approximately US$3 million/year. Vendor lock-in is acknowledged. Scarce ICT skills increase reliance on international contractors.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: A central national data repository is connected to all 37 district stations and 13 hospital-based registration centers in real time. The NIS is entirely digital with biometric data stored electronically. All stations have internet connectivity and computers.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2018 ID4D diagnostic describes a fully digital, real-time-linked national database, and a 2025 Institute of Development Studies report on Botswana's digital-ID describes Omang as a biometric platform incorporating fingerprint and facial recognition, corroborating continued electronic/digital record-keeping. Code 3 stands.

Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: ID4D 2018 data: 80-90% of the eligible population (age 16+) hold the Omang card (1,541,571 holders). Total population coverage is 67.3% (remaining 33% are mostly under 16 and thus not yet eligible). UNICEF reports 'over 90%' more recently. Coverage is in the 70-89% range for the eligible population per the primary ID4D diagnostic.

This places the score in the >89% band (code 5) rather than 70-89% (code 4); the original comment already flagged the UNICEF 'over 90%' figure, which this newer World Bank source now corroborates with an authoritative, dated figure.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
Comments: Omang is mandatory for accessing all social safety net programs. The Social Benefit Registration System (SOBERS) is directly linked to the NIS for beneficiary authentication. Programs including Old Age Pension (OAP), Destitute Persons Programme (DPP), and Orphans and Vulnerable Children (OVC) require Omang. Biometric authentication (fingerprints) is used for some programs.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. A 2022 World Bank social protection report confirms the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development's social registry is linked to the Omang ID system for validation, and the Government of Botswana's own Destitute Allowance guidance (gov.bw, current) requires a certified copy of the Omang as proof of nationality to apply. Code 3 (Mandatory) stands.
